claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of atomic short-range order.
Atomic size mismatch and preferential enthalpic interactions induce atomic short-range order.
Promoting nanometer-scale ordered domains enhances high-temperature strength.
Promoting nanometer-scale ordered domains enhances environmental resistance.
Promoting nanometer-scale ordered domains enhances radiation tolerance.
Promoting nanometer-scale ordered domains enhances cryogenic toughness.
A slight increase in Al content promotes atomic mobility and ordering under suitable thermal treatment.
Near-equilibrium thermal treatments permitting sufficient diffusion allow local ordering phenomena to emerge.
The proposed structural mediator is the formation and distribution of nanometer-scale ordered domains, including B2-type domains, within a disordered matrix.
Increased atomic size mismatch drives the formation of short-range ordered regions.
Selective bonding preferences drive the formation of short-range ordered regions.
Short-range ordered regions stabilize the single-phase structure at high temperatures.
Ordered regions provide barriers to dislocation motion.
Ordered regions provide barriers to defect propagation.
Samples with promoted local ordering will have higher high-temperature strength than the baseline.
Samples with promoted local ordering will have greater radiation tolerance than the baseline.
Samples with promoted local ordering will have greater cryogenic toughness than the baseline.
Modified samples will exhibit diffraction and microscopy signatures of nanometer-scale order.
Rapid quenching or other extreme non-equilibrium processing may suppress short-range order and limit the applicability of the hypothesis.
